Issued at 329 AM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

An omega blocking pattern persists over the CONUS early this 
morning, with the ridge axis situated over the Great Plains. 
This positioning allows for strong low level southerly return 
flow over the Northern Plains. A strong isobaric gradient 
between surface high pressure over the Mississippi River Valley 
and lee cyclogenesis along the eastern slopes of the Rockies has
maintained breezy southeast winds across western and central 
North Dakota through the night. A corridor of enhanced low level
moisture is maintained along the MT/ND border, mostly as a low 
stratus deck. But dense fog has recently returned to Bowman 
County after a middle of the night absence. Latest rapid-refresh
guidance shows high probabilities of dense fog spreading 
northward into Slope County, but not much further eastward into 
Hettinger or Adams Counties. Will keep the Dense Fog Advisory as
is for now, but the eastern 2 counties may be allowed to end 
early. The low stratus and fog should dissolve later this 
morning, but additional higher-based stratus could develop over 
central North Dakota later this afternoon and evening. Look for 
a mixture of sun and clouds today, with highs forecast in the 
lower 40s east to lower and mid 50s far west. Windy conditions 
are expected through this afternoon, out of the southeast 
around 20-30 mph and gusting to 30-40 mph.

From tonight into Sunday, a shortwave will eject from the 
Desert Southwest into the Southern Plains, undercutting the 
omega ridge. Meanwhile, a Canadian shortwave is forecast to 
eject from the Rockies into the prairie provinces. This will 
dampen the omega blocking and loosen the MSLP gradient, but 
maintain broad upper level ridging between the Great Plains and
Mississippi River Valley. This leads to a Sunday forecast with 
lighter winds, more plentiful sunshine, and warmer high 
temperatures around 50 degrees east to 60 degrees southwest. 
The upper ridge is forecast to slowly translate eastward early 
next week, leaving the Northern Plains under a southwest flow 
regime. Dry weather is expected through Tuesday, with well 
above average high temperatures in the lower 50s to lower 60s 
on Monday, slightly cooling to the upper 40s to mid 50s on 
Tuesday.

Forecast confidence is high that a western CONUS trough will 
eject into the Northern and Central Plains on Wednesday, but 
the strength of the wave and evolution of the surface pattern 
remain uncertain. There is broad consensus in lee cyclogenesis 
near the Black Hills early Wednesday, with the surface low 
tracking northeastward towards Lake Superior by midday 
Thursday. This would generally place most of North Dakota in 
the wrap-around deformation zone trailing the surface low, 
which is forecast to drag a cooler air mass into the region. 
Mid level forcing could take the form of a split flow regime, 
and there is latitudinal uncertainty in the northern stream. 
Furthermore, 00Z cluster analysis shows uncertainty in the 
progression of the wave. The total ensemble probability for 
measurable precipitation through Thursday afternoon is medium 
to high (around 60-80 percent), and probabilities for exceeding
a tenth of an inch range from around 30 percent southeast to 50
percent northwest. But there is one cluster showing a notably 
drier solution compared to the other three. The most likely 
timing of precipitation between sunset Wednesday and sunrise 
Thursday combined with the colder air advecting in introduces 
low chances for accumulating snow (at least 0.1 inch), ranging 
from around 10 percent in central North Dakota to 30 percent 
along the Montana border. 

Another deep trough is forecast over the western CONUS by 
Friday. From there, its evolution remains quite unclear. Two 
GEFS-heavy clusters composing around 45 percent of the total 
ensemble membership open up the wave, allowing strong synoptic 
forcing to spread over the Northern Plains by late Friday. The 
other 2 clusters that carry a majority of ECMWF and Canadian 
ensemble members form a cutoff low over the Great Basin. The 
former solution would favor a classic Colorado low that could 
impact the broader region Friday through Saturday. The latter 
solution would be more likely to keep Friday dry. But by late 
Saturday, the cutoff low scenario itself splits into two 
distinct outcomes: one that brings a stronger low into the 
Northern and Central High Plains and another that dissolves the
cutoff low over the Central Rockies. The former of those 2 
would be more likely to produce an impactful low pressure 
system over the weekend, while the latter would keep the 
highest QPF south of the state. It remains far too soon to draw

weather late next week into the weekend, and it is far from
